entries.meaning: To say something more after what has already been said. ---
examples: "And bring your passport," she added.
Would you like to add anything before we finish?
He has added a note at the bottom of the letter.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (add a comment), intransitive ("That's all," he added)

entries.meaning: To speak formally to a person or a group. ---
examples: The mayor will address the city council tonight.
She addressed the crowd from the steps of the library.
He was addressing the students when the fire alarm went off.
entries.contrast: The verb is always uh-DRES; the noun (where you live) is usually AD-res in American English.

entries.meaning: To agree, often unwillingly, that something bad or embarrassing is true. ---
examples: I admit I was wrong about the date.
She finally admitted that she had forgotten his birthday.
He has never admitted his part in it.
entries.contrast: The single t doubles before an ending: admit → admitted → admitting.

entries.meaning: To tell someone what you think they should do. ---
examples: The doctor advised him to rest for a week.
I'd advise you to read the contract twice.
She has been advising the company since January.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (advise students), intransitive (I would advise against it)
entries.contrast: advise is the verb and ends in a /z/ sound; advice is the noun and ends in /s/: "She advised me, so I took her advice."

entries.meaning: To have the same opinion as someone else, or to say yes to a plan. ---
examples: I agree with almost everything in her report.
They agreed to meet at the corner at noon.
We have never agreed about politics.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (I agree that it's late), intransitive (we all agree)
entries.contrast: Keep both e's and add nothing extra: agree → agreed → agreeing, never "agreeed" or "agred".

entries.meaning: To tell people about something officially or publicly. ---
examples: The airline will announce the new schedule on Friday.
They announced their engagement at dinner.
The winners have already been announced.

entries.meaning: To say you are sorry for something you have done. ---
examples: You should apologize to your sister.
He apologized for being late.
She left without apologizing.
entries.contrast: American spelling is apologize; British books write apologise. You apologize to a person for a thing.

entries.meaning: To disagree with someone in words, or to give reasons for an opinion. ---
examples: My neighbors argue about money every weekend.
She argued that the test was unfair.
They have been arguing since breakfast.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he argued that the law was unfair), intransitive (they argue constantly)
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: argue → arguing, not "argueing".

entries.meaning: To say something to someone in order to get an answer or a favor. ---
examples: Can I ask you something?
She asked me where the bathroom was.
Nobody has asked about the money yet.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (ask a question), intransitive (if you don't know, ask)
entries.contrast: In American English say /æsk/, not /ɑːsk/ — and ask me, never "ask to me".

entries.meaning: To tell someone confidently that something is true so that they stop worrying. ---
examples: I can assure you the package is on its way.
The nurse assured him that the pain would pass.
We have been assured that the water is safe.
entries.contrast: assure a person, ensure a result, insure a car: "I assure you the car is insured."

entries.meaning: To ask for something in a very urgent, humble way. ---
examples: Don't make me beg.
He begged her not to tell anyone.
The dog sat begging under the table.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she begged him to stay), intransitive (a man was begging on the corner)
entries.contrast: Double the g: beg → begged → begging.

entries.meaning: To say that someone or something is responsible for something bad. ---
examples: Don't blame the weather for your bad mood.
They blamed the driver for the accident.
I have never blamed you for what happened.
entries.contrast: You blame a person for a thing, or blame a thing on a person.

entries.meaning: To talk with too much pride about what you have or what you have done. ---
examples: He likes to brag about his car.
She bragged that she had finished in an hour.
They kept bragging all through dinner.
entries.contrast: Double the g: brag → bragged → bragging.

entries.meaning: To telephone someone, or to say someone's name loudly to get their attention. ---
examples: Call me when you land.
I called the office twice this morning.
Somebody has been calling and hanging up.
entries.русский: звонить, позвонить; звать, позвать; называть, назвать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (call your mother), intransitive (she called from the airport)

entries.meaning: To talk in a friendly, informal way. ---
examples: We can chat after the meeting.
They chatted in the parking lot for an hour.
She was chatting with a neighbor when I drove up.
entries.contrast: Double the t: chat → chatted → chatting.

entries.meaning: To talk quickly and continuously about unimportant things. ---
examples: The kids chatter the whole way to school.
She chattered nervously while we waited.
I could hear them chattering in the next room.

entries.meaning: To shout loudly to show support or approval. ---
examples: The whole stadium began to cheer.
They cheered when the power came back on.
A crowd was cheering outside the courthouse.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the fans cheered the team), intransitive (everyone cheered)

entries.meaning: To say that something is true even though it has not been proved. ---
examples: He claims he never got the email.
She claimed to be a doctor.
Two groups have claimed responsibility.

entries.meaning: To make something easier to understand by explaining it more fully. ---
examples: Could you clarify what you mean by "soon"?
The teacher clarified the instructions.
Nothing has been clarified yet.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: clarify → clarifies → clarified.

entries.meaning: To say or write something that gives an opinion about someone or something. ---
examples: The senator refused to comment.
Several readers commented on the photo.
He was commenting on the game when the signal cut out.
entries.contrast: You comment on something. The t is not doubled, because the stress is on KAH-: commented.

entries.meaning: To share information, ideas, or feelings with other people. ---
examples: The two departments barely communicate.
She communicated the bad news gently.
They have been communicating by email for years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (communicate your ideas clearly), intransitive (they communicate by text)

entries.meaning: To say that you are unhappy or annoyed about something. ---
examples: Guests often complain about the noise.
He complained to the manager.
She has been complaining all week.
entries.contrast: You complain about a problem to a person — never "complain on".

entries.meaning: To tell someone that you admire something about them. ---
examples: People always compliment her on her voice.
He complimented the chef on the sauce.
It felt good to be complimented in front of the whole team.
entries.contrast: compliment (praise) and complement (something that completes) sound alike but differ by one letter, i or e.

entries.meaning: To admit that you have done something wrong or embarrassing. ---
examples: I have to confess I've never read it.
He confessed after six hours of questioning.
She has confessed everything to her lawyer.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he confessed everything), intransitive (she finally confessed)
entries.contrast: A verb ending in -ss adds -es: confess → confesses.

entries.meaning: To say officially that something is true or definite. ---
examples: Please confirm your appointment by Friday.
The airline confirmed the flight this morning.
The rumor has not been confirmed.

entries.meaning: To tell someone that you are happy about their success or good luck. ---
examples: Let me congratulate you on the new job.
Everyone congratulated her after the show.
He left without congratulating the winner.
entries.contrast: You congratulate someone on something, and the t sounds like ch: kuhn-GRACH-uh-layt.

entries.meaning: To ask a person or a book for information or advice. ---
examples: You should consult a doctor about that cough.
She consulted her notes before answering.
They are consulting with the city about the permit.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (consult a lawyer), intransitive (he consults for two firms)

entries.meaning: To say the opposite of what someone else has said. ---
examples: Don't contradict your grandmother at the table.
His second story contradicted the first.
She has been contradicting herself all morning.

entries.meaning: To make someone believe something or agree to do something. ---
examples: Nothing you say will convince him.
She convinced me to try again.
I am not convinced that it is safe.

entries.meaning: To say what you think is wrong or bad about someone or something. ---
examples: It is easy to criticize from the outside.
The report criticized the hospital's record keeping.
He has been widely criticized for the remark.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they criticized the plan), intransitive (it is easy to criticize)
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ize; British books write criticise.

entries.meaning: To discuss a question formally, with people giving opposite opinions. ---
examples: The two candidates will debate on Tuesday.
Congress debated the bill for three days.
The issue is still being debated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they debated the bill), intransitive (the two sides debated for hours)

entries.meaning: To say something clearly, firmly, and often officially. ---
examples: "I'm not going," she declared.
Do you have anything to declare at customs?
The winner has not been declared yet.

entries.meaning: To say exactly what a word means or what something is. ---
examples: How would you define "success"?
The contract defined his duties clearly.
The border has never been clearly defined.

entries.meaning: To ask for something very firmly, as if you have a right to it. ---
examples: The workers demand a written answer.
She demanded to see the manager.
They are demanding an apology.
entries.contrast: demand takes no preposition: "He demanded an explanation," not "demanded for an explanation."

entries.meaning: To say that something is not true. ---
examples: He denies everything.
She denied taking the money.
The company has denied any wrongdoing.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: deny → denies → denied.

entries.meaning: To say what someone or something is like. ---
examples: Can you describe the man you saw?
She described the apartment over the phone.
The town has been described as sleepy.
entries.contrast: You describe something to someone: "Describe it to me," never "describe me it."

entries.meaning: To have a different opinion from someone else. ---
examples: I disagree with almost every word of that.
The two doctors disagreed about the treatment.
They have disagreed on this for years.
entries.русский: не соглашаться, не согласиться; расходиться во мнениях
entries.contrast: You disagree with a person and about or on a question.

entries.meaning: To say that something is not true or not fair. ---
examples: Nobody disputes that the road needs work.
She disputed the charge on her bill.
The results are still being disputed.

entries.meaning: To send someone a message by electronic mail. ---
examples: Email me the address when you get a chance.
I emailed her twice last week.
He has been emailing the whole department.
entries.русский: писать по электронной почте, написать письмо (по email)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (email me the file), intransitive (just email when you're ready)

entries.meaning: To give someone the confidence or the advice that makes them want to do something. ---
examples: Teachers should encourage questions.
My uncle encouraged me to apply.
She was encouraged by the early results.
entries.contrast: encourage someone to do something — the to is required.

entries.meaning: To say something suddenly and loudly because of surprise or strong feeling. ---
examples: "You're kidding!" she exclaimed.
Visitors always exclaim over the view.
He kept exclaiming how big the fish was.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive ("You're early!" he exclaimed), intransitive (they exclaimed over the view)

entries.meaning: To make something clear by describing it in detail. ---
examples: Could you explain the rules again?
She explained why the flight was canceled.
He has explained it three times already.
entries.contrast: You explain something to someone: "Explain it to me," never "explain me it."

entries.meaning: To put a thought or a feeling into words. ---
examples: It is hard to express how grateful we are.
She expressed her concerns in a short letter.
Several parents have expressed the same worry.

entries.meaning: To talk about other people's private lives, often unkindly. ---
examples: They gossip about everyone in the building.
We gossiped over coffee for an hour.
She caught them gossiping about her.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one p: gossiped, gossiping — the stress is on GAH-.

entries.meaning: To say hello to someone when you meet them. ---
examples: He greets every customer by name.
She greeted us at the door.
We were greeted by a very loud dog.

entries.meaning: To complain in a quiet, unhappy way. ---
examples: The drivers grumble about the new schedule.
He grumbled something and went back to bed.
She has been grumbling since we left.

entries.meaning: To suggest something indirectly instead of saying it openly. ---
examples: She hinted that she might quit.
Stop hinting and just tell me.
He has hinted at a bigger announcement.
entries.contrast: You hint at something: "He hinted at a raise."

entries.meaning: To suggest something without saying it directly. ---
examples: Are you implying that I lied?
Her tone implied that the answer was no.
Nothing in the letter implies a threat.
entries.contrast: The speaker implies; the listener infers. And the y becomes ie: implies, implied.

entries.meaning: To tell someone about something officially. ---
examples: Please inform the office of any change of address.
They informed us by letter.
We were never informed about the meeting.
entries.contrast: You inform someone of or about something.

entries.meaning: To ask for information, usually politely or formally. ---
examples: I called to inquire about the job.
She inquired whether the room was still free.
Several people have inquired about tickets.
entries.contrast: American English prefers inquire; British writing often spells it enquire.

entries.meaning: To say firmly that something must happen or is true, even when others disagree. ---
examples: He insists that he paid the bill.
She insisted on driving us home.
They kept insisting we stay for dinner.
entries.contrast: You insist on something: "She insisted on paying."

entries.meaning: To tell someone officially what they must do. ---
examples: The judge will instruct the jury this afternoon.
She instructed the class to put their phones away.
We were instructed to wait outside.

entries.meaning: To say something rude that offends someone. ---
examples: I didn't mean to insult anyone.
He insulted the waiter and we left.
She felt insulted by the question.
entries.contrast: The verb is in-SULT; the noun is IN-sult: "He insulted me, and it was a real insult."

entries.meaning: To start speaking while someone else is still talking. ---
examples: Please don't interrupt while I'm on the phone.
She interrupted him in the middle of a sentence.
I'm sorry for interrupting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't interrupt me), intransitive (sorry to interrupt)
entries.contrast: Two r's in the middle: interrupt.

entries.meaning: To ask someone questions, for a job or for a news story. ---
examples: They will interview five candidates on Monday.
A reporter interviewed the neighbors.
I'm being interviewed tomorrow at nine.

entries.meaning: To tell people someone's name when they meet for the first time. ---
examples: Let me introduce my brother.
She introduced herself to everyone at the table.
We have never been properly introduced.
entries.contrast: You introduce one person to another: "Introduce me to your friend."

entries.meaning: To ask someone to come to an event or to do something with you. ---
examples: Should we invite the neighbors?
They invited us to their wedding.
She wasn't invited, and she knows it.

entries.meaning: To say funny things that you do not mean seriously. ---
examples: Don't worry, I'm only joking.
He joked about his own cooking.
She jokes with the customers all day.

entries.meaning: To give a formal talk to a class or an audience, or to scold someone at length. ---
examples: She lectures on American history.
My father lectured me for an hour about the car.
I don't like being lectured about money.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (stop lecturing me), intransitive (he lectures at the state university)

entries.meaning: To say or write something about someone or something briefly. ---
examples: Did she mention where she was going?
He mentioned your name at lunch.
Your project was mentioned in the newsletter.
entries.contrast: mention takes a direct object with no preposition: "He mentioned the problem," never "mentioned about the problem."

entries.meaning: To laugh at someone in an unkind way, often by copying them. ---
examples: The other kids mocked his accent.
Don't mock people who are trying.
He was mocking the anchorman's voice.

entries.meaning: To speak quietly and unclearly, so that people cannot understand you. ---
examples: Speak up — you're mumbling.
He mumbled something about the traffic.
She mumbles when she is nervous.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he mumbled an apology), intransitive (stop mumbling)

entries.meaning: To say something in a soft, low voice. ---
examples: "Thank you," she murmured.
The crowd began to murmur.
They were murmuring in the back row.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she murmured his name), intransitive (the crowd murmured)

entries.meaning: To speak in a low voice, usually because you are annoyed. ---
examples: He muttered something rude under his breath.
She mutters at the television every night.
I could hear him muttering in the hallway.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he muttered a curse), intransitive (she muttered to herself)

entries.meaning: To keep asking or complaining about the same thing in an annoying way. ---
examples: Don't nag — I'll do it tonight.
She nagged him for weeks about the gutters.
He has been nagging me to call the dentist.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she nagged him about the bill), intransitive (stop nagging)
entries.contrast: Double the g: nag → nagged → nagging.

entries.meaning: To say what someone or something is called, or to give someone a name. ---
examples: Can you name all fifty states?
They named the baby after her grandmother.
A new director has been named.
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: name → naming.

entries.meaning: To talk with someone in order to reach an agreement. ---
examples: The union refuses to negotiate.
They negotiated a new lease last spring.
A deal is being negotiated right now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (negotiate a contract), intransitive (the two sides are negotiating)

entries.meaning: To mention something because it is important. ---
examples: Please note that the office closes at four.
The report noted several errors.
It should be noted that nobody was hurt.
entries.русский: отмечать, отметить; замечать (в речи или письме)

entries.meaning: To tell someone about something officially. ---
examples: We will notify you by mail.
The school notified the parents immediately.
Have the neighbors been notified?
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: notify → notifies → notified.

entries.meaning: To say that you do not agree with something or do not approve of it. ---
examples: If nobody objects, we'll start early.
Her lawyer objected twice in five minutes.
He left without objecting to a single word.
entries.contrast: The verb is uhb-JEKT; the noun (a thing) is AHB-jikt.

entries.meaning: To say that you are willing to give something or to do something. ---
examples: He offered to drive me to the airport.
They offer free coffee in the lobby.
She has been offered the job.
entries.contrast: One r only — the stress is on AW-: offered, offering, never "offerred".

entries.meaning: To tell someone firmly that they must do something. ---
examples: The judge ordered him to pay a fine.
You can't just order people around.
We were ordered off the field.

entries.meaning: To make someone decide to do something by giving them reasons. ---
examples: See if you can persuade her to come.
He persuaded the bank to wait a month.
I wasn't persuaded by the argument.
entries.contrast: persuade someone to do something — the to is required.

entries.meaning: To call someone on the telephone. ---
examples: Phone me when you get in.
He phoned the hotel from the airport.
She has been phoning all afternoon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (phone your mother), intransitive (she phoned to say she'd be late)

entries.meaning: To choose the words you use to say or write something. ---
examples: Let me phrase that differently.
He phrased the question very carefully.
The warning is phrased in plain English.

entries.meaning: To promise something seriously and publicly. ---
examples: The company pledged a million dollars.
Students pledge to follow the honor code.
The money has already been pledged.

entries.meaning: To say publicly that someone or something is very good. ---
examples: Reviewers praised the performance.
Don't be afraid to praise your kids.
The film has been praised everywhere.
entries.contrast: praise sounds exactly like prays: one is words of approval, the other is what you do in church.

entries.meaning: To give a religious talk, or to tell people how they should behave. ---
examples: He preaches at a small church downtown.
She preached patience and then lost her temper.
Stop preaching at me.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he preached a short sermon), intransitive (she preaches on Sundays)

entries.meaning: To say what you think will happen in the future. ---
examples: Nobody can predict the weather here.
She predicted the whole thing a year ago.
Snow has been predicted for Thursday.

entries.meaning: To tell someone that you will certainly do something. ---
examples: I promise I'll be there by six.
He promised to call and then didn't.
She has promised the car to her son.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (promise me one thing), intransitive (I promise)

entries.meaning: To make the sound of a word or a letter. ---
examples: How do you pronounce your last name?
She pronounced it the French way.
I have been pronouncing it wrong for years.
entries.contrast: The verb has -oun-, but the noun loses it: pronounce → pronunciation, never "pronounciation".

entries.meaning: To suggest a plan or an idea formally, or to ask someone to marry you. ---
examples: The city proposes a new bike lane on Main.
He proposed to her in a parking lot.
Several changes have been proposed.
entries.русский: предлагать, предложить; делать предложение (руки и сердца)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (propose a change), intransitive (he proposed on the bridge)

entries.meaning: To have an angry argument with someone. ---
examples: The brothers quarrel about everything.
They quarreled over a parking space.
She has been quarreling with the landlord for months.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: quarreled, quarreling; British writing doubles it, quarrelled.

entries.meaning: To ask someone questions, or to express doubt about something. ---
examples: Police questioned three witnesses.
Nobody questions her honesty.
He is being questioned at the station.

entries.meaning: To repeat the exact words that someone else said or wrote. ---
examples: Don't quote me on that.
The article quoted two city officials.
She has been quoted in every paper in the state.

entries.meaning: To say something that makes someone stop worrying. ---
examples: Try to reassure him before the surgery.
The pilot reassured the passengers.
I felt reassured after we talked.

entries.meaning: To say something aloud from memory. ---
examples: Each child had to recite a poem.
He recited the whole list without looking.
She was reciting the alphabet in the back seat.

entries.meaning: To tell someone that something is good and that they should try it. ---
examples: Can you recommend a good dentist?
She recommended the fish.
This brand has been recommended by three friends.
entries.contrast: One c but two m's: recommend.

entries.meaning: To say firmly that you will not do or accept something. ---
examples: They refuse to talk to reporters.
He refused the money.
She has refused every invitation this year.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he refused the offer), intransitive (she simply refused)
entries.contrast: The verb is rih-FYOOZ; the noun refuse (trash) is REF-yooss.

entries.meaning: To refuse to accept an offer, an idea, or a person. ---
examples: The board may reject the proposal.
They rejected my application twice.
His visa was rejected without explanation.
entries.contrast: The verb is rih-JEKT; the noun (a faulty item) is REE-jekt.

entries.meaning: To say something as a comment, without much emphasis. ---
examples: "It's colder than yesterday," he remarked.
Visitors often remark on how quiet it is.
Several people have remarked on the change.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he remarked that it was cold), intransitive (she remarked on his tie)

entries.meaning: To make someone remember something they have to do or know. ---
examples: Remind me to buy stamps.
She reminded him about the dentist.
You have reminded me three times already.
entries.contrast: You remind another person; you remember something yourself: "Remind me, because I never remember."

entries.meaning: To say or do something again. ---
examples: Could you repeat the question?
He repeated the number slowly.
She has repeated the same story all week.

entries.meaning: To answer someone in speech or in writing. ---
examples: He never replies to my texts.
She replied with a single word.
I'm still waiting for him to reply.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: reply → replies → replied. You reply to a person or a message.

entries.meaning: To give people information about something that has happened. ---
examples: Please report any damage to the office.
The paper reported that the school would close.
Two injuries have been reported.

entries.meaning: To ask for something politely or formally. ---
examples: You can request a later flight online.
She requested a window seat.
The song was requested by a listener in Ohio.
entries.contrast: As a verb, request takes no preposition: "He requested a copy," not "requested for a copy."

entries.meaning: To say or do something as an answer or a reaction. ---
examples: She hasn't responded to my email.
How did he respond to the news?
Firefighters were responding within four minutes.

entries.meaning: To tell people something that was secret or unknown. ---
examples: He refused to reveal his source.
The test revealed nothing unusual.
The winner will be revealed at nine.

entries.meaning: To speak angrily to someone because they did something wrong. ---
examples: She scolded the boys for tracking in mud.
Nobody likes to be scolded in public.
He scolds the dog and then feeds it anyway.

entries.meaning: To make a loud, high cry, usually from fear, pain, or excitement. ---
examples: Don't scream — it's only me.
She screamed when the lights went out.
The kids have been screaming in the pool all afternoon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she screamed his name), intransitive (the baby screamed)

entries.meaning: To say something very loudly. ---
examples: There's no need to shout.
He shouted something from the driveway.
They were shouting at each other in the hall.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he shouted a warning), intransitive (stop shouting)
entries.contrast: shout at someone means anger; shout to someone just means across a distance.

entries.meaning: To let out a long breath that shows you are tired, sad, or relieved. ---
examples: She sighed and picked up the phone.
He sighs every time I mention the garage.
"Fine," he said, sighing.
entries.contrast: The gh is silent: sigh rhymes with my.

entries.meaning: To say something exactly and clearly, leaving no doubt. ---
examples: Please specify the size and the color.
The letter didn't specify a date.
Unless otherwise specified, checkout is at eleven.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie: specify → specifies → specified.

entries.meaning: To say or write something clearly and definitely. ---
examples: Please state your name for the record.
The letter stated that the account was closed.
As stated above, the deadline is Friday.

entries.meaning: To say something with special force because it is important. ---
examples: I want to stress that this is not a punishment.
She stressed the word "today".
He kept stressing how little time we had.

entries.meaning: To speak with difficulty, repeating sounds at the beginning of words. ---
examples: He stutters a little when he is tired.
She stuttered through the first two sentences.
I was stuttering so badly that I gave up.

entries.meaning: To offer an idea or a plan for someone to think about. ---
examples: Can I suggest a different route?
She suggested that we leave early.
It has been suggested more than once.
entries.contrast: suggest never takes a person as its object: "She suggested a book to me," not "suggested me a book."

entries.meaning: To give the main points of something in a short form. ---
examples: Could you summarize the article in two sentences?
He summarized the meeting for those who missed it.
The findings are summarized on page four.
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ize; British books write summarise.

entries.meaning: To say things to someone as part of a conversation. ---
examples: We need to talk.
They talked for an hour in the driveway.
She has been talking about moving for years.
entries.contrast: The l is silent: talk is TAWK. You talk to or with a person about a thing.

entries.meaning: To make jokes about someone, either in a friendly or an unkind way. ---
examples: His brothers tease him about his hair.
She teased me for being nervous.
I'm only teasing.

entries.meaning: To send someone a short written message from a phone. ---
examples: Text me when you're outside.
He texted her twice and got no answer.
She has been texting all through dinner.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (text me the address), intransitive (she was texting in class)
entries.contrast: The past adds a whole syllable: texted is TEK-stid, two syllables.

entries.meaning: To tell someone that you are grateful for what they did. ---
examples: I want to thank everyone who helped.
She thanked the driver and got off.
He left without thanking anybody.
entries.contrast: You thank someone for something: "Thank you for the ride."

entries.meaning: To say that you will hurt or punish someone if they do not do what you want. ---
examples: He threatened to call the police.
Don't threaten me.
The workers are threatening a strike.
entries.contrast: The ea is short: THRET-uhn, like bread, not like treat.

entries.meaning: To change words from one language into another. ---
examples: Can you translate this for me?
She translated the whole contract in one night.
The book has been translated into forty languages.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (translate the letter), intransitive (she translates for the court)
entries.contrast: You translate from one language into another.

entries.meaning: To try hard to persuade someone to do something. ---
examples: Doctors urge everyone to get a flu shot.
She urged him to see a lawyer.
We are urging people to stay off the roads.

entries.meaning: To say something aloud, usually a single word or sound. ---
examples: He didn't utter a word all evening.
She uttered a small cry and sat down.
Those were the last words he ever uttered.

entries.meaning: To promise something very seriously. ---
examples: She vowed never to go back.
They vow to fight the decision in court.
He has vowed to finish the race.

entries.meaning: To tell someone about a danger or a problem so that they can avoid it. ---
examples: I'm warning you — that dog bites.
She warned us not to park there.
We had been warned about the traffic.
entries.contrast: warn sounds exactly like worn, the past participle of wear.

entries.meaning: To greet someone in a friendly way when they arrive. ---
examples: Please welcome our next speaker.
They welcomed us like family.
New members are always welcomed at the first meeting.

entries.meaning: To speak very quietly, using breath instead of voice. ---
examples: Why are you whispering?
He whispered something to the man beside him.
She whispers whenever she talks about money.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she whispered a name), intransitive (they whispered in the back)
entries.contrast: The h is silent: whisper is WIS-pur.

entries.meaning: To shout loudly, often in anger or to be heard far away.
examples: Don't yell at your brother.
Somebody yelled from across the street.
The coach was yelling the whole game.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he yelled my name), intransitive (don't yell)
entries.contrast: yell at someone is angry; yell to someone is just loud.
